Consonantal i

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

and conjunction

also and also, plus

classical

Cic. Att. 12.9.1: nec erat quod scrīberem, et somnus urgēbat

et

conjunction: joins words or clauses of equal weight

The plain “and”. Repeated, et … et is “both … and”. In narration it should not be the only joint between clauses: Latin ties actions together with a participle, an ablative absolute, a cum-clause or a relative, or sets them side by side with no word at all, as Caesar does (Hostēs terga vertunt; fugientibus equitēs occurrunt, B.G. 7.88). A single et between clauses with different subjects is classical (Cic. Att. 4.2.4); what sounds translated is et as the joint of every sentence. For “and not” Latin says nec.

Other words

  • -que — and (closely joined)

    enclitic conjunction, added to the first word of the second member · also used · classical · Cato Agr. praef. 2: bonum agricolam bonumque colōnum

    Joins two things that belong together, or adds the last member of a pair: diēs noctēsque, day and night; terrā marīque, by land and sea (Lewis & Short).

  • atque (ac) — and also, and indeed

    conjunction: atque before vowels and consonants, ac only before consonants · also used · classical · Catull. 101.10: frāter, avē atque valē; Cic. Att. 16.6.4: dēliciīs atque amōribus meīs

    Joins closely, with weight on what is added; often two near-synonyms (Lewis & Short: “a close internal connection”, where et joins different things). Etiam atque etiam, again and again.

Examples

  • nec erat quod scrīberem, et somnus urgēbat

    there was nothing to write, and sleep was pressingCic. Att. 12.9.1

  • virum bonum quom laudābant, ita laudābant: bonum agricolam bonumque colōnum

    when they praised a good man, they praised him like this: a good farmer and a good husbandmanCato Agr. praef. 2

  • nam mihi ante oculōs diēs noctēsque versāris

    for you are before my eyes day and nightCic. Fam. 14.2.3

  • Cicerō bellissimus tibi salūtem plūrimam dīcit. etiam atque etiam valē.

    our lovely Cicero sends you his warmest love. Goodbye, again and again.Cic. Fam. 14.7.3

  • frāter, avē atque valē

    brother, hail and farewellCatull. 101.10

  • Hostēs terga vertunt; fugientibus equitēs occurrunt.

    The enemy turn and run; the cavalry meet them as they flee. (Two clauses with no “and”.)Caes. B.G. 7.88

See also both … and, and not, also, therefore.
